{{Short description|Demographic statistical analysis}}
{{Essay-like|date=July 2026}}
[[Population decline]] has many potential effects on individual and national [[economy]]. The single best gauge of economic success is growth in [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] per capita, not GDP.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2008/03/13/grossly-distorted-picture|title=Grossly Distorted Picture|last=|first=|date=May 13, 2008|newspaper=The Economist}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|title=Solving the paradox|url=https://www.economist.com/special-report/2000/09/23/solving-the-paradox|last=|first=|date=September 23, 2000|newspaper=The Economist}}</ref> GDP per capita is an approximate indicator of average living standards, for individual prosperity.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|url=https://ourworldindata.org/economic-growth|title=Economic Growth|last=Roser|first=Max|date=2019|journal=Our World in Data}}</ref> Therefore, whether population decline has a positive or negative economic impact on a country's citizens depends on the rate of growth of GDP per capita, or alternatively, GDP growth relative to the rate of decline in the population.<ref name=":0"/>

==Background==

The simplest expression for the size of a country's economy is

{{block indent|1=GDP = total population × GDP/person<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|title=The Role of Population in Economic Growth|journal=SAGE Open|volume=7|issue=4|pages=215824401773609|last=Peterson|first=E. Wesley|date=October 11, 2017|doi=10.1177/2158244017736094|doi-access=free}}</ref>}}

GDP/person is also known as [[Gross domestic product#GDP per capita|GDP per capita]] or per capita GDP. This term is a simple definition of [[Productivity#Labour productivity|economic productivity]] as well as individual [[standard of living]].

The real change in total GDP is defined as the change in population plus the real change in GDP/capita.<ref name=":2"/> The table below shows that historically, for every major region of the world, both of these have been positive. This explains the enormous economic growth around the world brought on by the [[Industrial Revolution|industrial revolution]]. However, the two columns on the right also show that, for every region, population growth in the future will decline and, in some regions, go negative. The table also shows that two major economies, Japan and Germany, may face the same conditions.

Because

{{block indent|1=GDP = total population × GDP/person,}}
as populations grow more slowly, assuming no changes in growth of GDP/person, GDP will also grow more slowly.

== If per capita GDP increase is less than the decrease in total population ==
The equation above shows that if the decline in total population is not matched by an equal or greater increase in productivity (GDP/capita), and if that condition continues from one calendar quarter to the next, it follows that a country would experience a decline in GDP, known as an economic recession.

The possible impacts of a declining population that leads to permanent recession are:

# '''Decline in basic services and infrastructure.''' If the GDP of a community declines, there is less demand for basic services such as hotels, restaurants and shops. The employment in these sectors then suffers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED066250.pdf|title=The Causes and Consequences of Rural Depopulation: Case Studies of Declining Communities|last=Wallace|first=P. J.|date=August 1972|website=US Department of Health Education and Welfare}}</ref> A falling GDP also implies a falling tax base that would support basic infrastructure such as police, fire and electricity. The government may be forced to abandon some of this infrastructure, like bus and railroad lines, and combine school districts, hospitals and even townships in order to maintain some level of [[economies of scale]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|title=Who's afraid of population decline? A critical examination of its consequences|last=Coleman|first=David|journal=Population and Development Review|date=January 25, 2011|volume=37|issue=Suppl 1|pages=217–248|doi=10.1111/j.1728-4457.2011.00385.x|pmid=21280372|citeseerx = 10.1.1.702.6098}}</ref>
# '''Rise in dependency ratio.''' [[Dependency ratio]] is the ratio of those not in the [[labor force]] (the ''dependent'' part ages 0 to 14 and 65+) and those in the labor force (the ''productive'' part ages 15 to 64). It is used to measure the pressure on the productive population. Population decline caused by [[sub-replacement fertility]] rates means that every generation will be smaller than the one before it. Combined with longer life spans the result can be an increase in the dependency ratio which can put increased economic pressure on the work force. With the exception of Africa, [[Dependency ratio#Total dependency ratio by regions|dependency ratios]] are forecast to increase everywhere in the world by the end of the 21st century.
# '''Crisis in end of life care for the elderly.''' A falling population caused by sub-replacement fertility and/or longer life spans means that the growing size of the retired population relative to the size of the labor force, known as [[population ageing]], may cause a crisis in end of life care for the elderly because of insufficient caregivers for them.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2018-02-09/americans-will-struggle-to-grow-old-at-home|title=Americans Will Struggle to Grow Old at Home|last=Kim|first=Tammy|date=February 9, 2018|website=Bloomberg Businessweek}}</ref>
# '''Difficulties in funding entitlement programs.''' Population decline can impact the funding for [[Social security|programs for retirees]] if the ratio of working age population to the retired population declines. For example, in Japan, there were 5.8 workers for every retiree in 1990 vs 2.3 in 2017 and a projected 1.4 in 2050.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/joelkotkin/2017/02/01/death-spiral-demographics-the-countries-shrinking-the-fastest/#7d7ef5a8b83c|title=Death Spiral Demographics: The Countries Shrinking The Fastest|last=Kotkin|first=Joel|date=February 1, 2017|website=Forbes}}</ref> Also, according to new research (2019) China's main state [[pension fund]] will run out of money by 2035 as the available workforce shrinks due to effects of that country's [[one-child policy]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-economy/article/3005759/chinas-state-pension-fund-run-dry-2035-workforce-shrinks-due|title=China's state pension fund to run dry by 2035 as workforce shrinks due to effects of one-child policy, says study|last=Tang|first=Frank|date=April 12, 2019|website=South China Morning Post}}</ref> With the exception of Africa, [[Dependency ratio#Total dependency ratio by regions|this trend prevails]], to a greater or lesser extent, everywhere else in the world.
# '''Decline in military strength.''' Big countries, with large populations, assuming technology and other things being equal, tend to have greater military power than small countries with small populations. In addition to lowering working age population, population decline will also lower the military age population, and therefore military power.<ref name=":3" />
# '''Decline in innovation.''' A falling population also lowers the rate of innovation, since change tends to come from younger workers and entrepreneurs.<ref name=":4" />
# '''Strain on mental health.''' Population decline may harm a population's mental health (or morale) if it causes permanent recession and a concomitant decline in basic services and infrastructure.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Economic downturns and population mental health: research findings, gaps, challenges and priorities|last=Zivkin|first=K.|date=2011|journal=Psychological Medicine|volume=41|issue=7|pages=1343–1348|doi=10.1017/S003329171000173X|pmid=20836907|pmc=3846090}}</ref>
#'''Deflation.''' A recent (2014) study found substantial deflationary pressures from Japan's ageing population.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2016/12/31/Is-Japans-Population-Aging-Deflationary-41812|title=Is Japan's Population Aging Deflationary?|last=Anderson|first=Derek|date=August 4, 2014|website=International Monetary Fund}}</ref>
# '''Unemployment.''' A Slovenian study from 2015 found that population ageing leads to higher rates of unemployment and less entrepreneurial activity.<ref>{{cite web |title=Impact of Population Ageing on Unemployment and Entrepreneurial Activity: the Case of Slovenia |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/287359978 |access-date=23 December 2020}}</ref>

==If GDP per capita increase is greater than population decrease==
The single best gauge of economic success is growth in GDP per person, not total GDP.<ref name=":0"/> GDP per person, also known as [[Gross domestic product#Lists of GDP per capita|GDP per capita]], is a simple definition of individual [[economic productivity]] as well as a rough proxy for average [[Standard of living|living standards]], for individual prosperity.<ref name=":1"/> 

If a nation can focus on increasing the [[Population decline#Increase the productivity of the workforce|productivity of its citizens]], that improvement in economic output will help increase its GDP. It will also increase the average standard of living of its people because higher economic output per person usually produces higher household incomes.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |date=Sep 23, 2000 |title=Solving the paradox |url=https://www.economist.com/special-report/2000/09/23/solving-the-paradox |website=The Economist}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=Mar 4, 2020 |title=How well does GDP per capita really measure our well-being? |url=https://businesscouncilab.com/insights-category/analysis/how-well-does-gdp-per-capita-really-measure-our-well-being/#:~:text=The%20reason%20this%20is%20such,those%20working%20in%20that%20economy. |website=Business Council of Alberta}}</ref> By increasing its GDP per capita, a  country can therefore increase its average living standard even though its population growth is low or even negative, and if it can increase GDP per capita faster than its population is declining, it can also increase its total GDP.

Consider for example Japan. As the table below shows, even though Japan's population declined 2.0% during the period 2012-2022, its per capita GDP, a rough approximation of the overall productivity of the Japanese people, rose by about 7.5%, a much greater increase than the 2.0% decrease in its population. As a result its GDP still grew by 4.7%, and the increase in GDP per capita produced a higher standard of living for the Japanese people.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" />

The UN projects that Japan's population decline will accelerate to about −0.7% per year in the 2040–2045 time period.<ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=World Population Prospects 2022, Standard Projections, Compact File, Variant tab, Population growth rate column |url=https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/Standard/MostUsed/ |website=United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division. |access-date=2023-03-06 |archive-date=2022-07-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711213112/https://population.un.org/wpp/Download/Standard/MostUsed/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> This means that for Japan's GDP to grow during that period, per capita GDP growth must be greater than 0.7% per year.

One analysis of data for forty countries shows that while low fertility will indeed challenge government programs and very low fertility undermines living standards, moderately low fertility and population decline favor the broader material standard of living.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ntaccounts.org/web/nta/show/Science|title=Is Low Fertility Really a Problem?|last=|first=|date=2014|website=National Transfer Accounts}}</ref>
